topic: What would happen to an unprotected human on Mars

sources.title: Ask an Astrophysicist: space travel archive (human exposure to vacuum; the 1965 suit-leak accident)
sources.publisher: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Imagine the Universe! (HEASARC)
sources.note: Answers by NASA volunteers; the 1965 account is written by a scientist at NASA's Manned Spacecraft Center.

sources.title: Human Exposure to the Vacuum of Space
sources.cites: NASA and US Air Force decompression research, 1950s-60s

claims.text: Mars' surface air pressure is about 6.36 millibars, less than 1% of Earth's (1,014 mb): a very thin atmosphere.
claims.quote: Surface pressure: 6.36 mb at mean radius (variable from 4.0 to 8.7 mb depending on season); Surface pressure: 1014 mb; is a dusty, cold, desert world with a very thin atmosphere

claims.text: Mars' air is about 95% carbon dioxide.
Below about 6.3 kPa (47 mmHg, about a sixteenth of sea-level pressure), water boils at body temperature (37°C); Mars' surface pressure is about a tenth of that.
claims.quote: at an ambient pressure of 6.3 kilopascals (47 mmHg) , the boiling point of water is 37 °C (99 °F) . A pressure of 6.3 kPa—the Armstrong limit—is about 1/16 of the standard sea-level atmospheric pre; the vapor pressure of water at 37 C is 47 mm Hg; Surface pressure: 6.36 mb at mean radius
claims.note: 6.36 mb = 0.636 kPa; 6.3 / 0.636 = 9.9, so Mars is about ten times below the Armstrong limit.

claims.label: simplified: for your body, close to a vacuum
claims.text: Because Mars' pressure is far below the Armstrong limit, exposed body fluids on Mars behave much as in a vacuum; we use NASA's vacuum-exposure accounts for it (simplified).
claims.quote: saliva , tears , urine , and the liquids wetting the alveoli within the lungs—but not vascular blood (blood within the circulatory system)—will boil away if the subject does not wear a full-body pressure suit

claims.text: Your blood would not boil, because your skin and circulatory system contain it (blood pressure keeps it above 47 mmHg).
claims.quote: You do not explode and your blood does not boil because of the containing effect of your skin and circulatory system; As long as you keep your blood-pressure above that (which you will unless you go deep into shock) your blood will not boil; but not vascular blood

claims.text: The saliva on your tongue would start to boil.
claims.quote: The saliva on your tongue might boil, however; saliva , tears , urine , and the liquids wetting the alveoli within the lungs

claims.text: Holding your breath in a vacuum is likely to damage your lungs.
claims.quote: Holding your breath is likely to damage your lungs

claims.text: A person exposed to vacuum stays conscious for about 10 to 15 seconds, about the time oxygen-poor blood takes to reach the brain.
claims.quote: concluded that a human exposed to a vacuum will remain conscious for ten to fifteen seconds; He remained conscious for about 14 seconds, which is about the time it takes for O2 deprived blood to go from the lungs to the brain

claims.text: In 1965, at NASA's Manned Spacecraft Center, a test subject was exposed to near vacuum when a space suit leaked in a vacuum chamber; he stayed conscious about 14 seconds, his last memory was the water on his tongue beginning to boil, and he regained consciousness as the chamber was repressurised.
claims.quote: At NASA's Manned Spacecraft Center (now renamed Johnson Space Center) we had a test subject accidentally exposed to a near vacuum (less than 1 psi) in an incident involving a leaking space suit in a vacuum chamber back in '65. He remained conscious for about 14 seconds; we began repressurizing the chamber within 15 seconds. The subject regained consciousness at around 15,000 feet equivalent altitude; his last conscious memory was of the water on his tongue beginning to boil

claims.text: Mars' average temperature is about minus 59°C.
You would not instantly freeze: heat does not transfer away from a body quickly.
claims.quote: You do not instantly freeze because, although the space environment is typically very cold, heat does not transfer away from a body quickly

myths.myth: In a vacuum (or on Mars without a suit) your blood boils and you explode.
myths.truth: Your skin and circulatory system keep your blood under pressure: no boiling blood, no exploding; exposed fluids like saliva do boil (NASA).

open_questions: Mars is not a hard vacuum (about 0.6 kPa); the NASA accounts are for near vacuum. The page labels this as a simplification.
The 1965 test subject is not named or drawn.
